summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been lawful in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate crime and hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation are criminalised. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, and reported discrimination is described as rare; one travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal only in certain contexts, which conflicts with the country overviews reporting no general prohibition.

Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added sexual orientation to Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (5 years).

The provisions cited in the sources name sexual orientation; none of them names gender identity. A trans visitor has no equivalent statutory protection on the face of the text.

Enforcement is documented. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for five days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man.

Legal gender recognition is not available. Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking placed Monaco 45th of 49 European countries. A trans visitor's identity documents will not correspond to any Monegasque recognition procedure, because none exists.

Partner recognition is limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry; cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax rather than like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Monegasque law, none of these routes produces spousal recognition.

Anti-discrimination legislation has repeatedly failed. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme in every year of the primary and secondary cycles to sensitise pupils against racism and the other article 1 discriminations, including sexual orientation. The Council of Government did not approve the bill, and the replacement introduced on 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Visibility is low. Roughly ten people are openly out in Monaco, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is described as limited. Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo, a Council of Europe rapporteur, described the position as the sad record of Monaco.

There is no Pride in Monaco and no official gay bars, clubs or events; visitors travel to France or Italy for Pride, and the nearest comparable scenes are in Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report for Monaco recorded no significant changes and no reports of torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses. The significant issues it identified were the libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking placed Monaco 45th of 49 European countries, near the bottom of the regional table.

Monaco's position sits between the French legal regime it is economically tied to and its own more limited protections. The nearest cities with an organised scene, Marseille, Nice and Lyon, are in France, and Monegasque visitors seeking Pride events cross into France or Italy.

Monaco is not a member of the European Union, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, despite strong cultural and economic ties with France.
localsOnly:
Residents in a same-sex relationship may sign a contrat de vie commune. The agreement was introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019, and came into force on 27 June 2020, six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco. It is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry.

The agreement does not produce spousal treatment. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, no survivor pensions and no parental leave, and same-sex couples have no right to adopt.

Transgender residents cannot alter their legal gender. No administrative or judicial route to legal gender recognition is described in the sources.

Community infrastructure is absent. No Pride is held in Monaco, there are no official gay bars, clubs or events, and roughly ten people are openly out. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support.

Anti-discrimination protection for sexual orientation and gender identity is not in force. The 2011 bill's article 44 school-sensitisation requirement was not approved by the Council of Government, and the 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources conflict on the scope of anti-discrimination law. The Outright International overview reports that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, while a travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal in certain contexts. The specific contexts, if any, are not identified in the inventory.

No enforcement data is available for the 2019 amendments to the Civil Code, and no trans-specific violence figures for Monaco were identified in the sources.

The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's full text and the reasons the Council of Government withheld approval are not sourced.

Whether any Monegasque provision addresses gender identity in hate-crime or hate-speech terms is not established by the sources; the cited articles name sexual orientation only.
